items.name: 10 Downing Street
clues: From the front it looks like an ordinary Georgian terraced house. Behind the famous black door, it’s much bigger than it looks.
About 100 rooms, including offices and state dining rooms, plus a small flat upstairs that some recent residents swapped for the bigger one next door.
Westminster, London, a few minutes’ walk from Parliament, on a street closed to the public behind iron gates.
Robert Walpole, usually called Britain’s first prime minister, moved in in 1735.
The resident cat, Larry, holds the official title of Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office.
The British prime minister’s official home: the number between 9 and 11.

items.name: Graceland
clues: An elegant 1930s mansion with white columns, bought in 1957 for just over $100,000 by a 22-year-old who had just become very rich.
The most famous room is the Jungle Room, with green shag carpet on the floor and on the ceiling.
Memphis, Tennessee.
The couple who built it named it after an aunt called Grace. Its most famous resident lived here until 1977 and is buried in the garden.
Hundreds of thousands of fans visit every year, some of them in rhinestone jumpsuits and very large sideburns.
The home of Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll.

items.name: Neuschwanstein Castle
clues: A fairy-tale property on a rock above a gorge, commissioned by a king who preferred dreams to politics.
Many of the planned rooms were never finished, but there is a throne room, a hall for singers and an artificial cave.
Bavaria, near Füssen, close to the Austrian border.
Its owner lived here for only about 170 days before his death in 1886. It opened to paying visitors within weeks.
Walt Disney is said to have used it as the model for a castle in Disneyland.
King Ludwig II’s castle. Its name means “new swan stone”.

items.name: Buckingham Palace
clues: A substantial London townhouse, bought by a king in 1761 as a family home for his wife. Extended once or twice since.
775 rooms, including 52 bedrooms for the family and guests, 188 bedrooms for staff and 78 bathrooms.
Central London, overlooking a park, at the end of a wide red road used for parades.
Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live here, from 1837.
The grand State Rooms open to visitors in the summer. On special occasions, the family waves from the balcony.
The King’s London home, named after the duke who built the house it grew out of.

items.name: 221B Baker Street
clues: First-floor rooms in a London house, shared by two single men, with a very patient landlady downstairs.
A cosy sitting room with a violin, chemistry experiments and tobacco kept in the toe of a Persian slipper.
Marylebone, London, near Regent’s Park and a famous wax museum.
Its most famous tenant first moved in in a novel published in 1887, together with an army doctor.
A museum on the street uses the number, although it really stands at number 239. The BBC filmed its version in a different street.
Sherlock Holmes’s address.

items.name: The White House
clues: A grand neoclassical home built of grey sandstone painted a famous colour. Rebuilt after British troops set fire to it in 1814.
132 rooms and 35 bathrooms on six levels, plus a cinema, a bowling alley and an office with no corners.
In a capital city on the Potomac river, built specially to be the seat of government.
Its main resident has always held the same job, since 1800. Only the first person to hold that job never lived here.
New residents usually move in on 20 January, every four or eight years.
The US president’s home, at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.
